summary: A 1942 L-4 cab on Garwood Butte, renamed in 1946, went unstaffed after 1973 and is now in poor condition at the end of a steep trail.

facts.design: L-4 cab, an updated BC-301 version
facts.status_note: Standing, but no longer staffed and described by the Forest Service as in poor condition.

access.note: Reached by the Garwood Butte Trail from Three Lakes Road (Road 3703) and Forest Service Road 3703-370. The Forest Service warns the structure is in poor condition.

visit.trail_note: Steep, rocky trail with narrow switchbacks; footing is difficult on the last few feet of the climb.

facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service, Umpqua National Forest

events.note: L-4 cab, an updated BC-301 version, built on the summit then called Bear Butte.
Butte and lookout renamed for Leroy E. Garwood (firelookout.com and Oregon Hikers both give 1946).
No longer staffed after 1973, per the register. Firelookout.com says abandoned since the 1960s.
Firefighters covered the whole cabin in Structure Protection Wrap.
Added to the National Historic Lookout Register, June 23, 2022.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Firelookout.com and the Oregon Hikers guide both date the renaming to 1946. The Forest Service page gives Garwood's death year (1944) but no renaming year. The story uses 1946.
The register says the lookout was no longer staffed after 1973. Firelookout.com says it has been abandoned since the 1960s. The story reports both.

Firelookout.com says restoration has been ongoing in recent years. The Oregon Hikers guide says restoration efforts have stopped, and it calls its own information anecdotal. The story reports both and does not settle the question.

Sources describe him as a former Umpqua National Forest employee (firelookout.com), an administrative officer of the forest (Oregon Hikers), and a former Diamond Lake District Ranger (Forest Service).

notes_for_editor: The renaming year (1946 on two sites), the end of staffing (1973 in the register, 1960s on firelookout.com) and restoration status all conflict and are reported as such. The brief's L-4 design is kept; the register adds that the cab is an updated BC-301 version. A search snippet from cherylhill.net gives 1944 for the renaming; that page was not read in full, so it is not used. Restoration status is the most likely to be stale and should be rechecked before publishing. Access is marked public for the trail only; the sources do not say whether the cabin can be entered, and the Forest Service warns about its condition, so the story does not encourage entry.
